top_level_objectives: Understand vectors as quantities with magnitude and direction, and learn to represent them algebraically and geometrically
Master vector addition (tip-to-tail method) and decomposition into orthogonal components
Apply trigonometry to relate a vector's magnitude and direction to its component values
Understand how projectile motion emerges from the independent combination of constant horizontal velocity and uniformly accelerated vertical motion
Predict and explain how launch angle and initial speed affect projectile range, maximum height, and flight time

scenes.scene_name: Introduction to Vectors as Abstract Objects
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce students to the geometric representation of vectors in 2D space and establish the concepts of magnitude and direction.
key_visuals: A single vector arrow displayed in 2D space, with adjustable length and angle
A coordinate grid with labeled x and y axes
Text labels showing magnitude (numerical value) and direction (angle in degrees or compass bearing)
Interactive slider controls for adjusting magnitude and angle
student_actions: Observe and manipulate a vector's magnitude by dragging its tip
Rotate the vector through different angles and observe how direction changes
Read and interpret the displayed magnitude and angle values
Predict how magnitude and direction change before dragging the vector

scenes.brief_purpose: Teach vector addition geometrically by placing vectors tip-to-tail and observing the resultant vector.
key_visuals: Two colored vector arrows (e.g., red and blue) in the same 2D space
A third vector (resultant, e.g., green) showing the sum of the two vectors
A dashed parallelogram or triangle showing the geometric relationship
Numerical labels showing the magnitude and direction of each vector and the resultant
student_actions: Drag the tail of the second vector to the tip of the first vector
Observe the resultant vector emerge from tail of first vector to tip of second
Swap the order of the two vectors and confirm the resultant remains the same (commutativity)
Predict the magnitude and direction of the resultant before seeing the numerical values

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how a single vector can be decomposed into horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components along a coordinate system, introducing the concept of component vectors.
key_visuals: A single vector arrow at an arbitrary angle in a 2D coordinate system
Two component vectors (one horizontal, one vertical) shown with a right triangle construction
Right triangle with legs labeled Vx and Vy, and hypotenuse labeled V
Numerical values for each component and the original vector's magnitude
student_actions: Observe the vector decomposition for multiple launch angles
Drag the original vector to change its angle and watch the component vectors adjust
Identify which component changes as the angle increases from 0° to 90°
Recognize that the three vectors (original and two components) form a right triangle

scenes.scene_name: Relating Components to Magnitude and Direction Using Trigonometry
scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the mathematical relationships between a vector's magnitude, direction angle, and its orthogonal components using trigonometry.
key_visuals: A right triangle with the hypotenuse labeled as vector V (magnitude), acute angle labeled θ (direction)
Component vectors and right triangle sides labeled Vx and Vy
Displayed equations: Vx = V cos(θ), Vy = V sin(θ), and V = √(Vx² + Vy²)
An angle protractor or degree scale showing the relationship visually
student_actions: Input a magnitude and angle and calculate the components using the displayed formulas
Verify the calculations by observing the drawn vectors
Work backward: given two component values, determine the magnitude and angle
Test trigonometric relationships for special angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)

scenes.scene_name: Introduction to Projectile Motion: Decomposing Initial Velocity
scenes.brief_purpose: Connect vector concepts to physics by decomposing an initial velocity vector into horizontal and vertical components for a projectile launched at an arbitrary angle.
key_visuals: A launch platform with a projectile at rest
An initial velocity vector at an adjustable launch angle, decomposed into Vx and Vy components
A coordinate system with the launch point at the origin
Text labels for initial speed, launch angle, Vx, and Vy
student_actions: Adjust the launch angle and observe how the vertical component Vy increases and horizontal component Vx decreases
Set specific launch angles (e.g., 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°) and record the component values
Predict the initial velocity components for a given angle before adjusting the simulation
Recognize that the magnitude of the initial velocity vector remains constant as only the angle changes

scenes.scene_name: Observing Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that horizontal and vertical motions evolve independently by comparing the projectile's trajectory to simultaneous horizontal and vertical displacement lines.
key_visuals: A projectile trajectory drawn as a parabolic curve
A horizontal reference line moving at constant velocity equal to Vx
A vertical reference line (or motion indicator) showing the changing vertical position under constant acceleration due to gravity
Vectors showing instantaneous velocity decomposition at multiple points along the trajectory
Time markers or snapshots at regular intervals showing the projectile's position
student_actions: Launch a projectile at a fixed angle and observe the parabolic path
Pause the simulation at regular time intervals and identify the horizontal and vertical displacements separately
Confirm that the horizontal displacement increases linearly with time (constant velocity)
Confirm that the vertical displacement follows a parabolic relationship (constant acceleration)
Drag the initial velocity vector to change Vx or Vy and predict how the trajectory changes

scenes.scene_name: Exploring the Effect of Launch Angle on Range and Height
scenes.brief_purpose: Allow students to systematically vary the launch angle and observe how this parameter affects the projectile's range (horizontal distance) and maximum height.
key_visuals: A launch platform with adjustable angle indicator (protractor or angle slider)
A trajectory curve that updates as the angle changes
Ground reference line with distance markers for measuring range
Vertical height markers and a label showing maximum height reached
A superposition of multiple trajectories for different angles (e.g., 30°, 45°, 60°) shown in different colors for comparison
student_actions: Launch projectiles at various angles (15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°) and record the range and maximum height for each
Identify the angle that produces the maximum range and compare it to the theoretical prediction (45° in ideal conditions)
Observe that complementary angles (e.g., 30° and 60°) produce the same range but different maximum heights
Predict the range and height for an untested angle before launching

scenes.scene_name: Exploring the Effect of Initial Speed on Range and Height
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how initial speed (magnitude of initial velocity) affects the projectile's range and maximum height while keeping the launch angle fixed.
key_visuals: A launch platform with an adjustable speed control (slider or numerical input)
Multiple trajectory curves displayed simultaneously, each corresponding to a different initial speed
Trajectory curves in different colors, clearly distinguished and labeled with their initial speeds
Distance and height markers showing how range and maximum height increase with speed
Numerical displays of range, maximum height, and flight time for each speed
student_actions: Launch projectiles at a fixed angle (e.g., 45°) with varying initial speeds
Measure and record the range and maximum height for each speed tested
Observe the qualitative pattern: as speed increases, both range and maximum height increase
Test whether doubling the initial speed doubles the range, and explain why or why not (based on the mathematics of projectile motion)
Compare the trajectories visually and identify which trajectory reaches higher and farther
